prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and for transforming the analysis of exporting, reallocation and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: I now put B038 first. Melitz (2003) shifted trade analysis from countries and industries to firms. It explains exporter selection, within-industry reallocation and a productivity channel for the gains from trade. It gave empirical researchers a framework that fits customs and production microdata. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, and his broader firm-level trade theory, makes the pair a coherent core. Over two decades the framework has been tested on many datasets and has spread into macro, IO and development. Credit is more concentrated here than for B015: two names carry most of the identifiable theoretical contribution. Eight of the eleven opening rankings include the candidate and seven place it in the top three, though I do not treat that as scientific merit. My opening first choice, B035 (BLP and dynamic industry models), is mature and has been used far beyond IO, but I cannot make a clean three-name attribution given Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin. No colleague ranked it, and my enthusiasm may reflect my own field. I keep it as an alternative, not the preferred part.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation on B038 is attribution and novelty. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made major contributions to the same literature but are not credited names. Krugman's 2008 prize already recognised the earlier new trade theory, and the quantitative gains-from-trade magnitudes depend on elasticity and model assumptions. Helpman also appears under B030, so any recognition would need to be accounted for once. B015 has broader practical influence on central banking than B038 has on trade policy. If the committee judges policy and conceptual influence to outweigh attribution cleanliness, B015 is a defensible first choice.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B038 first. He sees a large conceptual break with strong empirical discipline, a natural successor to the 2008 prize. He favours crediting Melitz and Helpman over Redding, but he flags the credit split with Helpman's trade-politics work and the sensitivity of gains-from-trade results to elasticities.
responses.response: I agree on a Helpman-Melitz pairing rather than adding Redding. Redding's quantitative and spatial work extends the framework and is not the founding contribution. I would qualify the empirical claim. The firm-level facts on exporter premia were documented before the model, and the model explained them. The strongest confirmation is therefore the selection and reallocation mechanism, not the size of the welfare gains, which depend on elasticity assumptions. I would not let the citation rest on a particular gains-from-trade number. The citation I propose emphasises selection and reallocation for that reason. On Helpman's presence in B030, I agree it needs one-time accounting. I see no reason it should weaken the case under B038.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B015 first. He credits staggered contracts and pricing (Taylor, Calvo) and Woodford's microfounded synthesis with large, durable influence on theory and central-bank practice. He acknowledges that omitting Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets is a real cost.
responses.response: I agree B015 has very large practical influence, and I keep it as an alternative. I differ on how readily it can be turned into a prize. Calvo's pricing rule, Taylor's contracts and rule, and Woodford's synthesis are different kinds of contribution, separated by decades. A three-name set leaves out others the chair himself says have strong claims. My own survey and transaction-level work on price adjustment makes me cautious about reading Calvo pricing as an empirical finding. It is a tractable device, and the micro evidence on time-dependent versus state-dependent adjustment is mixed. That does not undermine its influence, but it makes a citation praising the pricing foundations harder to write. I note my IJIO 2026 co-authorship with Hassler on menu costs in the conflict note.

responses.point: Krusell calls B015 the strongest case on the list. He cites its changes to academic macroeconomics and central-bank thinking, its full maturity, and its survival through the financial crisis and the post-2021 inflation, with attribution as the main difficulty.
responses.response: I accept the influence and maturity. Where I differ is on how much weight the framework's survival through 2008 and 2021-23 should carry. Persistence of a workhorse framework shows it is useful and adaptable. It is weaker evidence that the specific building blocks credited to three people were confirmed. That gap is the attribution problem Krusell names, and I give it more weight than he does. If the committee wants a macro prize, I would want the discussion to settle the citation first, either policy rules and staggered contracts or the integrated framework. Otherwise the three-name set looks arbitrary.

uncertainties: Whether Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum have claims strong enough that a Helpman-Melitz prize would be seen as under-crediting the literature.
Whether the committee judges that the 2008 prize on new trade theory reduces the case for another trade award.
Whether the committee would prefer a Melitz-Helpman-Redding grouping or a narrower two-name set.
Whether B015 should rank above B038 if attribution can be settled around a clear citation.
How far my industrial-organisation and international-pricing background biases my weighting of firm-level trade and of B035.
statement.conflict_note: From the supplied profile: I co-authored a 2026 IJIO paper on menu costs and price adjustment with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen. Hassler ranks B015 first, which I treat as an alternative, not my preferred part. I am married to Magdalena Andersson, a public fact that the profile says has no evidence of bearing on committee work. My research field (international pricing, trade, IO) is close to B038, B035 and the pricing side of B015, but I find no co-authorship or institutional tie to Helpman, Melitz, Redding or the other credited names on B035 and B015. No recusal-requiring connection is apparent from the supplied profile, and I disclose these ties without adjudicating them.
